item.title: The cost of simulating classically tractable quantum circuits and dynamics
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Polynomial-time classical simulations of quantum dynamics are often outpaced by direct quantum hardware execution due to high one-time quantum sampling and shadow post-processing overheads when preparing unknown input states.

Grade 0.492 · 2.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Su Yeon Chang, Supanut Thanasilp, Zoë Holmes, M. Cerezo

Figure

Estimated total wall-clock time versus qubit count n for direct quantum simulation and classical simulation across IonQ Forte, Google Sycamore, and IBM Heron architectures.

Asks

Whether classically simulable quantum evolutions are in practice more resource-efficient to simulate classically or to execute directly on quantum hardware.

But

Independent unentangled input copies only (no multi-copy quantum memory); unitaries and observables restricted to efficient classical representations.

Tools

classical shadows · Lie-algebraic simulation (g-sim) · Pauli Propagation · Majorana Propagation · hardware pricing models

Abstract

Determining whether a quantum evolution can be efficiently simulated classically is central to understanding the boundary between classical and quantum computation. However, polynomial-time simulability is an asymptotic statement, and does not by itself determine whether the (quantum-inspired) classical simulation is actually practical. Indeed, different polynomial scalings can lead to vastly different computational costs, particularly when expensive preprocessing or quantum data acquisition is required. In this work, we ask whether classically simulable quantum dynamics are in practice more resource-efficient to simulate classically than to execute directly on quantum hardware. We analyze this question using three resource metrics, quantum sample, quantum time, and classical time complexity, for several widely studied classically simulable circuit families. Using representative hardware-level estimates, we identify regimes in which quantum simulation can be faster despite the existence of a polynomial-time classical algorithm, as well as regimes in which classical simulation remains more efficient. At the same time, the large quantum sampling cost needed to characterize unknown input states can make this polynomial-time classical simulation prohibitively expensive with current cloud-based hardware access prices. Ultimately, our work indicates that guarantees of classical simulability with polynomial resources alone are insufficient to determine the preferred implementation.

item.title: A Quantum-Inspired Dequantization Method for Diagonally Weighted Matrix Functions: Application to Learning with Optimized Random Features
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Classical algorithm samples from the optimized random feature distribution within total variation distance dTV(𝒟ϵ,𝒟′)≤δ in runtime O(Dpolylog⁡(G)+𝐪(𝑸(τ))+𝐬𝐪(𝒒ˆ(ρ)))×O~((Qmax⁡(τ)/ϵ)18/δ6), dequantizing the QSVT-based sampler.

Grade 0.477 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum singular value transformation and beyond: exponential improvements for…” · Natsuto Isogai, Mio Murao, Hayata Yamasaki

Figure

Schematic of the dequantization method: sampling from SQ(𝑫) isolates heavy diagonal indices to truncate 𝑫 to 𝑫~, reducing γ𝑰+𝑫~𝑨𝑫~ to a small principal block 𝑴~S computed classically.

Asks

Can quantum machine learning algorithms for matrix functions of diagonally weighted matrices be classically dequantized when sampling access is available only to the diagonal factor rather than the composite matrix?

Before

Quantum sampler ran in time O(Dlog⁡(G)log⁡log⁡(G)+𝐪(𝑸(τ))+𝐬𝐪(𝒒ˆ(ρ)))×O~((Qmax⁡(τ)/ϵ)polylog⁡(1/δ)), while standard classical matrix inversion required time exponential in D (GD×GD matrix).

But

Runtime scales polynomially as 1/δ6 rather than quantum polylogarithmic dependence polylog⁡(1/δ); assumes SQ(𝑫) and Q(𝑨) oracle access.

Tools

diagonal truncation via heavy-index sampling · principal submatrix restriction · rejection sampling · noisy matrix entry estimation

Abstract

Quantum-inspired classical algorithms have dequantized several quantum machine learning routines by replacing quantum linear-algebra subroutines with classical counterparts. However, the sampler based on quantum singular value transformation (QSVT) for learning with optimized random features is not covered by existing dequantization frameworks, because the matrix to be inverted is not itself available through sampling access. In this work, we develop a classical algorithm to address this type of quantum-advantage candidate. Our method samples heavy indices, reduces the transformation to a small principal block, and outputs a sparse classical representation with operator-norm guarantees. Applying this method dequantizes the sampler for optimized random features, giving a classical sampler with prescribed accuracy and polynomially related runtime. These results show that the factorization underlying a quantum block encoding can itself provide sufficient classical structure even when sampling-and-query access to the composite matrix is unavailable.

item.title: Distributed variational quantum computing with deterministic entanglement tuning
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Distributed variational quantum computing protocol deterministically tunes shared Bell-pair entanglement via LOCC with unit success probability (pM=1) and concurrence 𝒞M(θ)=cos⁡θ, keeping state infidelity below 0.05 across full range.

Grade 0.416 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “A variational eigenvalue solver on a photonic quantum processor” · Ilhwan Kim, Yong-Su Kim, Kwang Jo Lee, Hyukjoon Kwon, Yosep Kim, Hyang-Tag Lim

Figure

Concurrence (top) and state infidelity (bottom) plotted against the tuning angle θ, demonstrating deterministic modulation of entanglement from 1 down to 0 while keeping state infidelity below 0.05.

Asks

How can entanglement between distributed quantum processing units be tuned continuously and deterministically without the probabilistic losses of filtering or the high Bell-pair consumption of gate teleportation?

But

Demonstrated on bipartite single-qubit photonic processors; feed-forward conditional operations performed offline rather than in real time; pure-state majorization requires initial entanglement to be equal to or greater than target.

Tools

spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) · displaced Sagnac interferometer · POVM with path-mode ancilla · COBYLA optimization · quantum state tomography

Abstract

Distributed quantum computing offers a scalable route to quantum information processing by entangling spatially separated processors. Although gate teleportation enables universal computation across distributed nodes, it requires repeated consumption of high-fidelity Bell pairs, ancillary qubits, and real-time feedforward, which imposes significant overhead and reduces fidelity. However, many variational quantum algorithms do not demand full universality; rather, they rely on sufficient expressibility to explore solution spaces effectively. Building on this, we propose a distributed variational quantum computing protocol based on deterministic entanglement tuning. In contrast to probabilistic filtering, our approach deterministically modulates pre-shared entanglement using only local operations and classical communication. We validate the protocol through a proof-of-principle experiment by estimating ground-state energies of the He-H⁺ molecule and the Schwinger model, showing that diverse entanglement levels can be engineered to match problem-specific requirements. Our results suggest a practical alternative for near-term distributed quantum applications.

item.title: Optimal T-Count for Block Encodings of Fermionic and Spin Hamiltonians
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Worst-case block-encoding T-count scales as Θ(n2log⁡(n4/ε)) for general second-quantized fermionic Hamiltonians and Θ(n+log⁡(1/ε)) for bond-dependent Kitaev honeycomb spin Hamiltonians.

Grade 0.410 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Hamiltonian Simulation by Qubitization” · Jiaxin Ma, Kevin J. Joven, Yuan Liu

Figure

Plots T-gate count versus number of spin orbitals n for molecular electronic Hamiltonians in STO-3G basis, comparing the theoretical lower bound against existing block-encoding implementations.

Asks

What is the asymptotically optimal worst-case T-count required to construct an ε-approximate block encoding of structured fermionic and spin Hamiltonians?

Before

For fermionic Hamiltonians, upper bound was O(n2log⁡(n4/ε)) (Liu 2024), but matching lower bounds and spin-Hamiltonian optimal scalings were unknown.

But

Unitary Clifford+T model without mid-circuit measurements or classical feed-forward. Bounds are worst-case over the full coefficient family and do not exploit specific molecular structure.

Tools

ancilla compression theorem · volume-covering and circuit counting · stabilizer nullity monotonicity · linear combination of unitaries (LCU)

Abstract

We determine the non-Clifford T-gate cost of constructing block encodings of structured fermionic and spin Hamiltonians in a unitary Clifford+T model, when arbitrarily many clean ancillas and unrestricted block-encoding subnormalization are allowed, but without mid-circuit measurements or classical feed-forward. Our main technical tool is an ancilla-compression theorem: any block encoding of an n-qubit operator with a clean ancillas and at most s T gates can be compressed to use at most mina,n+2s ancillas, without increasing the absolute error or T-count. For general second-quantized Hamiltonians with bounded one- and two-body coefficients, at operator-norm block-encoding error ε, a volume-covering argument combined with circuit counting gives the worst-case lower bound Ω(n²√log(n⁴/ε)), matching the existing upper bound at fixed precision. For the bond-dependent Kitaev honeycomb family on n spins, we obtain independent lower bounds Ω(n) from stabilizer nullity and Ω(log(1/ε)) from one-qubit state preparation, established using different Hamiltonian instances. Together with an explicit LCU construction, they give the tight worst-case scaling Θ(n+log(1/ε)). As an application, we evaluate the T-count of a Hamiltonian simulation circuit based on quantum singular value transformation, with each block-encoding query compiled separately. When phase synthesis and controlled queries add at most constant-factor overhead, the simulation T-count scales as the query count times the optimal T-count per query.

item.title: Virtual quantum neural networks
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Extending quantum neural networks to linear combinations of completely positive trace-preserving maps via sampling and classical post-processing mitigates hardware noise and recovers ground-state energy curves under depolarizing noise.

Grade 0.407 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum singular value transformation and beyond: exponential improvements for…” · Benchi Zhao, Xuanqiang Zhao, Yinan Li, Yingzhou Li, Giulio Chiribella

Figure

Calculated ground state energy of HeH+ plotted against nuclear separation. Increasing the sampling budget from standard VQE (γ=1) to VVQE with γ=1.5 and γ=2.5 pulls noisy estimates back to the exact error-free curve.

Asks

Can quantum neural networks enlarge their optimization space beyond completely positive trace-preserving maps using randomized sampling and classical post-processing to boost expressivity and noise robustness?

Before

Standard QNNs and VQEs are restricted to a single parametric completely positive map (‖𝒄‖1=1), yielding inaccurate energies under circuit noise.

But

Demonstrated in numerical simulations under depolarizing noise (p=0.01 single-qubit, p=0.02 two-qubit), depth d=5, and Chebyshev truncation K=100.

Tools

Virtual quantum neural networks (VQNN) · Virtual variational quantum eigensolver (VVQE) · Truncated Chebyshev polynomial negativity approximation · Probabilistic circuit sampling

Abstract

Quantum neural networks are a prominent model of quantum machine learning. Their training consists in the minimization of a given loss function over a parametrized family of quantum circuits, mathematically described by unitary operators, or, more generally, completely positive linear maps. In this work, we extend the notion of quantum neural network, using random sampling and classical data processing to enlarge the optimization space in a way that includes linear combinations of completely positive maps. Our extended model, called virtual quantum neural networks, leverages its enlarged optimization space to achieve increased expressivity and improved noise robustness. These benefits are illustrated in three representative tasks: quantum error mitigation, binary classification, and estimation of ground-state energies. Overall, virtual quantum neural networks offer a flexible learning paradigm that expands the space of achievable computations and strengthens the applications of near-term quantum hardware.
